title: Token bucket and sliding windows
idea: A rate limiter's core is per-key state plus one rule: a token bucket spends tokens that refill over time, while window algorithms count recent calls.

analogy.text: A water jug under a dripping tap. You pour a cup per request; the tap refills slowly, and the jug overflows past full.
analogy.breaks: Our bucket refills only when someone checks it, not continuously.

points: Token bucket refills lazily: on each call, add tokens for the time elapsed.
Integer milli-tokens avoid floating-point drift in long-running buckets.
Fixed windows let a burst through on both sides of a window edge.
Sliding log is exact but stores one timestamp per allowed call.

hero.title: Token bucket: capacity 3, one per second

steps.caption: At t=0 a new key starts with a full bucket. Four calls arrive together.
Call 1 spends one token and is allowed.
Calls 2 and 3 spend the last two tokens. Bursts up to capacity pass at once.
Call 4 finds the bucket empty. It is rejected with a wait until one token returns.
At t=1500 the next call arrives. Refill runs first: 1500 ms since t=0 adds 1.5 tokens.
The next call spends one token. Half a token stays for later.
After a long idle gap, refill stops at capacity. The next burst is still capped at 3.

code.title: Token bucket
code.caption: A complete token bucket with lazy refill, integer math, and a retry-after hint, driven by a manual clock.

walk.text: Capacity 3, one token per second, four calls at time zero.
Call again at 500 ms, at 1500 ms, and after a minute idle.
Store milli-tokens as a long, so half a token is exactly 500.
Each key owns a bucket: its tokens and the time of its last refill.
Refill lazily: ms elapsed times tokens per second is exactly milli-tokens, capped at capacity.
With a whole token available, spend it and report what is left.
Otherwise compute how long until one whole token exists, rounded up.

code.title: Three window algorithms
code.caption: Same limit, same traffic: four calls per 1000 ms around a window edge. Here `tryAcquire` returns a boolean only so the three algorithms can be counted side by side.

walk.text: Three limiters, each allowing four calls per 1000 ms window.
Send bursts of four at 900, 1000 and 1950 ms, and count the allowed calls.
Fixed window: reset the count at each aligned start, then compare with the limit.
Sliding log: drop timestamps older than one window from the front.
If the log is still full, reject; otherwise record this call.
Sliding counter: on a new window, the old current count becomes previous.
Weight the previous count by its overlap with the sliding window, in integers.

pitfalls: Do not refill with a background thread per key; refill lazily on each call.
Avoid double for tokens; drift adds up. Use integer milli-tokens instead.
Fixed windows can allow twice the limit across an edge; say so in interviews.

quiz.q: What does the first line of Windows print?
quiz.why: 900 and 1000 fall in different aligned windows, so both bursts pass: eight calls in 100 ms. The 1950 burst shares the full second window.

takeaway: Token bucket allows bursts up to capacity; sliding windows smooth out window edges.
